Article Text:

NEW DELHI: India's warm-up match against a Sri Lanka XI ahead of the two-Test series has been shortened from four days to three days, the Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC) confirmed. The practice match will now be played from August 7 to August 9 at the Nondescripts Cricket Club (NCC) Ground in Colombo.In a statement, SLC said: "Team India will play a 3-day warm-up game instead of the originally scheduled four-day fixture. The warm-up fixture will commence on 7 August at the NCC Grounds, Colombo. The India team is scheduled to arrive in Sri Lanka on 4th August. The first Test will be played at the Galle International Cricket Stadium (GICS) from 15 to 19 August, while the second Test will be held at the SSC, Colombo, from 23 to 27 August.SLC did not reveal why the duration of the warm-up match was reduced.After the practice game, India will begin the two-match Test series against Sri Lanka.The first Test will be played in Galle from August 15 to 19, while the second Test will be held in Colombo from August 23 to 27.The series is part of the ongoing World Test Championship (WTC) cycle.BCCI had announced a four-day practice matchWhen the Indian squad was announced, the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) had said: "Ahead of the series, the team will play a four-day practice match in Colombo, starting on August 7."
Article Summary: India's warm-up match against a Sri Lanka XI has been shortened from four days to three days. The practice match will now be played from August 7 to August 9 at the Nondescripts Cricket Club (NCC) Ground in Colombo. The India team is scheduled to arrive in Sri Lanka on 4th August. The first Test will be played at the Galle International Cricket Stadium (GICS) from 15 to 19 August.

Article Title: The promise, the pain and the gold: Asmita Dey's journey to Commonwealth Games history
Article Text:
Asmita Dey (PTI Photo)

Father's dream



The debt



Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The beginning



NEW DELHI: As Asmita Dey walked into SEC Hall 4 for the women's 48kg judo final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, she looked around for one familiar face. Standing there was her coach, Yashapal Solanki.Minutes later, Asmita defeated Canada's Heidi Quach by yuko to become the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal. She came from behind to force the contest into Golden Score - judo's version of sudden-death extra time - before landing the decisive yuko to seal a historic victory.After the final, Asmita walked straight towards Solanki and hugged him. Both were in tears.Solanki was not Asmita's father. But after she lost her own father, he stepped into that role when she needed someone the most.A visibly emotional Asmita remembered both men after creating history."Papa jaane se pehle keh gaye the ki tum apne sapne ko aage badhana. Mere papa hamesha mujhe support karte the. Beech mein mujhe injury hui thi, tab papa mere liye Delhi aaye the. Dawai, ilaaj, sab kuch unhone hi sambhala tha. I dedicate this medal to my coach Solanki sir, my father, who passed away in December 2025 [Before he passed away, my father told me to keep chasing my dreams.He always supported me. When I got injured, he came to Delhi for me and took care of my treatment. I dedicate this medal to my coach Solanki sir and to my father, who passed away in December 2025]," Asmita had told reporters after winning the gold medal.Her father, Arjun Dey, who ran a cycle repair shop in Tripura, passed away in December, leaving Asmita heartbroken. She even thought of quitting the sport.After attending the funeral and the last rites, Solanki convinced her that fulfilling her father's dream was the best way to honour him.Apart from dealing with the emotional loss, Asmita was also battling a Grade-2 ankle injury.She returned to training at the Sports Authority of India centre in Bhopal under Solanki before moving to his academy in Delhi to continue her preparations. It was not easy. During training, memories of her father often overwhelmed her, and she would break down."The day after the 13th-day rituals for her father were completed, she came to Delhi. Two days later, we took her to France to prepare for the Commonwealth Games. She didn't stop after that. I was worried too, but she always kept telling me, 'Papa ka sapna poora karna hai'," Solanki told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview from Birmingham.The injury made the challenge even tougher."She suffered an injury before the Commonwealth Games. Surgery was discussed, so we sought second and third medical opinions. The doctors said that if she pushed herself a little, she could still compete. We decided to give it a try. She won the gold despite competing with a Grade-2 injury," Solanki said."The doctors had warned that the injury would trouble her repeatedly. She felt the pain several times during the bouts, but she never gave up."For Solanki, it was another reminder of the resolve she had shown through the toughest phase of her life."Her commitment is on another level. She is competing at a different level now. She cannot be stopped. Whensomeone loses a loved one, fear no longer remains. She is no longer afraid," he said.As grief and injury weren't enough, financial hardship also threatened Asmita's journey.During the Covid lockdown, her father struggled to support the family through his bicycle repair shop. To keep the household running, he borrowed money on interest. Over time, the debt snowballed into a substantial financial burden that the family found impossible to clear.People kept coming to the house demanding repayment, but the family had little means to pay them back."The family had borrowed money on interest, and creditors kept harassing her father," Solanki said.When Solanki learnt about the family's financial condition, he decided to step in."When I came to know about it, I told her not to worry about a single rupee. I repaid the money."He then made a promise to Asmita's mother that went far beyond the role of a coach."I have promised her mother that she is like my daughter and I will also perform her kanyadaan," he said.Solanki also ensured Asmita could continue focusing on judo."She got a constable's job in UP Police, but that salary was not enough to manage training, food and support the family. Now she has become a sub-inspector," he said.Born in Belonia, Tripura, Asmita was initially an 800-metre runner.Solanki first noticed her during the Khelo India Games. When he learnt about her interest in judo, he brought her under his guidance."The best part is that she is now an international player, and even goes abroad for training, but she is still in touch with her childhood coaches. That's the quality of this girl," Solanki signed off.
Article Summary: Asmita Dey is the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal. She came from behind to force the contest into Golden Score - judo's version of sudden-death extra time - before landing the decisive yuko to seal a historic victory. Her father, Arjun Dey, passed away in December, leaving Asmita heartbroken.

Athletics and para athletics produce another rich medal return

India enjoyed its most successful day of the 2026 Commonwealth Games on Saturday, collecting a remarkable 16 medals to climb to fourth in the overall standings with 39 medals (13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze). The campaign was powered by a record-breaking boxing performance, where Indian pugilists captured seven gold and three silver medals, while podium finishes also came in para athletics, athletics and judo. Beyond the medals, Indian athletes remained active across cycling, bowls and track and field, with several campaigns ending while others produced encouraging performances despite narrowly missing the podium.Indian boxing produced one of the country's finest Commonwealth Games performances, winning 10 medals from 10 finals after every semifinalist converted their guaranteed podium finish into either gold or silver.Sakshi Chaudhary opened the golden run by defeating England's Ruby White to claim the women's 51kg title. Preeti Pawar followed with victory over Canada's Scarlett Savannah Delgado in the women's 54kg final, while Jaismine Lamboria overcame Northern Ireland's Michaela Walsh to secure gold in the women's 57kg category.Priya Ghanghas added another title by beating Canada's Marie-Bathoul Al-Ahmadieh in the women's 60kg final before Arundhati Choudhary defeated England's Chantelle Reid to become Commonwealth champion in the women's 70kg division.India's success extended to the men's events as Sachin Siwach defeated Namibia's Tryagain Morning Ndevelo to win gold in the men's 60kg final, while Ankush Panghal completed the golden collection with victory over England's Dimeji Shittu in the men's 80kg final.There were also three silver medals. Lovlina Borgohain finished runner-up after losing the women's 75kg final to Australia's Emma Sue Greentree. Jadumani Singh settled for silver in the men's 55kg final after defeat to Australia's Jye Dixon, while Narender Berwal claimed silver in the men's 90kg final after losing to England's Damar Thomas.The 10-medal boxing campaign marked India's biggest highlight of the Games and played the central role in the country's climb up the medal table.India added six more medals across athletics, para athletics and judo.In the men's F57 shot put, Soman Rana produced a season-best throw of 13.40m to win gold, finishing 0.12m ahead of compatriot Shubham Juyal, whose season-best 13.28m earned silver and completed an Indian one-two. Cameroon's Cedric Azamdzi finished third with 12.57m.The men's triple jump also produced a double podium. Praveen Chithravel claimed silver with a best leap of 16.58m, finishing behind Jamaica's Jordan Scott, who won gold with 16.72m. Selva Prabhu Thirumaran secured bronze with 16.52m to ensure India occupied two places on the podium.Gulveer Singh added another athletics medal by taking bronze in the men's 5,000m in 13:24.95. Australia's Ky Robinson claimed gold, Kenya's Michael Kiplangat Kipsang finished second, while Gulveer held off Kenya's Cornelius Kemboi by just 0.04 seconds to secure third place.Judo also contributed through Unnati Sharma, who defeated South Africa's Skye Knoester by ippon in just one minute and seven seconds to win bronze in the women's -63kg category.India also had a busy day in events that did not produce medals.Harsh Tokas kept his medal hopes alive in the men's -81kg judo by defeating Samoa's Peniamina Percival in the repechage before falling to Australia's Keishin Ochi in the bronze-medal contest.Karanjit Singh Maan saw his men's -90kg campaign end after losing to Scotland's Scott Cusack in the repechage, while Inunganbi Takhellambam exited the women's -70kg competition after defeat to England's Jemima Yeats-Brown in the repechage.In the women's 10,000m race walk, Priyanka Goswami narrowly missed a podium finish in fourth place, while Ravina Gayakwad was disqualified.India's pole vault challenge also concluded without a medal as Dev Meena and Kuldeep Kumar finished outside the podium positions in the men's final.Para athlete Ramesh Shanmugam finished seventh in the men's T54 1500m final.India reached the mixed 4x400m relay final after the quartet of Vishal T.K., Rajesh Ramesh, Rashdeep Kaur and Neeru Pathak safely negotiated the heats. For the final, Ansa Babu replaced Rajesh Ramesh and Santhosh Kumar Tamilarasan came in for Neeru Pathak, joining Vishal T.K. and Rashdeep Kaur. The revised quartet finished sixth in 3:20.32, with Jamaica taking gold in 3:10.97 ahead of England (3:11.58) and Nigeria (3:12.85).Track cycling brought a series of early exits. David Beckham Elkatohchoongo, Ronaldo Singh Laitonjam and Rojit Singh were all eliminated during the men's sprint qualification, while Dinesh Kumar and Harshveer Singh Sekhon did not finish the men's 10km scratch race qualifying event.India's bowls campaign also came to an end. The men's pairs team of Navneet Singh and Dinesh Kumar lost to England in sectional play and were knocked out of medal contention, while Nayanmoni Saikia suffered defeat to South Africa's Bridget Herselman in the women's singles sectional match.With the Games concluding on Sunday, India will have one final opportunity to add to its tally of 39 medals. The country's hopes rest with track cycling, where Dinesh Kumar, Harshveer Singh Sekhon, Ronaldo Singh Laitonjam and Lisha Das will compete in the velodrome, and judo, where Ishroop Narang, Avtar Singh and Yash Ghanghas will aim to finish India's Glasgow campaign on a high.
Article Summary: India enjoyed its most successful day of the 2026 Commonwealth Games on Saturday, collecting a remarkable 16 medals to climb to fourth in the overall standings with 39 medals (13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze) The campaign was powered by a record-breaking boxing performance, where Indian pugilists captured seven gold and three silver medals. podium finishes also came in para athletics, athletics and judo.

Article Title: Bobby Fischer: The champion America summoned, and Iceland sheltered
Article Text:
Bobby Fischer

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

(Aarav Dengla is India’s 93rd Grandmaster. He is a keen observer and student of the world history in general and chess history in particular)

The Laugardælir Church near Selfoss is so easy to miss that I had to find it using Google Maps. A small white timber building and a scatter of headstones in the southern Icelandic quiet, an hour or so from Reykjavík, ringed by nothing but farmland. This is the final resting spot of Bobby Fischer, one of the greatest chess players ever.I went to visit his grave in the summer of 2024—an International Master chasing the rating that would make me a Grandmaster, half hoping the ground might lend me some of what its occupant had. The headstone had a simple cross, his name (Robert James Fischer) and his date of birth and date of death. No epithets, no words. Occasional visitors had left candles and chess pieces at the grave. As I stood in the bone-chilling Icelandic wind, I was moved. Here lay one of the chess’s greatest minds—marked only by a modest stone and a few offerings left by visitors. My brain was a jumble of thoughts about the transience of fame, belonging and life itself. My father, who was accompanying me, eventually nudged me to leave. We drove for the next hour in silence. He was also in a reflective mood.Everyone knows Bobby Fischer for the genius he was. Few fully know the arc of his life and appreciate his impact on chess.Rewind to 1972, and to this same island. In Reykjavík, a twenty-nine-year-old from Brooklyn sat down against Boris Spassky, the Soviet world champion, in a world championship duel. By then chess had become the Cold War condensed onto sixty-four squares, and Fischer very nearly did not play. He quarreled over the money, the cameras and the venue itself. Among those who persuaded him to go was Henry Kissinger, President Richard Nixon's national security adviser, who reportedly told him: "America wants you to go over there and beat the Russians. " Fischer played. He ended twenty-four years of Soviet dominance and became, overnight, a national hero in America.That aspect of his life everyone knows. It was immortalized in 2014 biopic Pawn Sacrifice where Tobey Maguire played Bobby Fischer. The movie ended on a positive note when Fischer beat Spassky in 1972. But Fischer’s legacy extends far beyond that match.It was Fischer who, in 1989, patented the chess clock that adds time after every move; helping players avoid losing winning positions solely to frantic time scrambles. Versions of Fischer’s increment system are now widely used in elite tournaments, including World Championship matches. It was Fischer who devised Fischer Random Chess (popularly known as Chess960) in which back-rank pieces are rearranged under specific constraints to reduce dependence on memorized opening theory. His primer, Bobby Fischer Teaches Chess, introduced generations of beginners to basic tactical and mating patterns. There is a subtler bequest, the one usually written off as Fischer’s tantrum: his furious demands over prize money and playing conditions before the 1972 championship led to increase in the prize money at chess tournaments. The record purse of 1972, doubled at the eleventh hour to get Fischer to play, was only the start. Every grandmaster who has since made a living from the game owes a little to Fischer.What came afterward is harder to confront. Fischer withdrew into isolation and increasingly expressed paranoid, antisemitic and other hateful views—words that cannot be defended or erased by admiration for his chess. Various writers have speculated about his mental health. Sadly, those utterances eclipsed his achievements.More ignominy lay waiting. Two decades after Kissinger's call, the same country that had once summoned him to fight Soviets issued a warrant for his arrest. For playing a 1992 rematch against Spassky in Yugoslavia, in defiance of American sanctions. The hero was now a fugitive. He drifted through exile, was detained for months in Japan for attempting to travel on a passport that American authorities had revoked. He faced deportation to United States and possibility of imprisonment there.That his detention did not end in deportation to the United States was due largely to a determined campaign by his Icelandic supporters. A handful of Icelanders, some who still remembered his 1972 triumph, campaigned to free him. The Icelandic parliament voted to grant him citizenship. The small nation that had staged his finest hour would not let him die a man without a country. Iceland took him in, and in time gave him the quiet resting spot where chess players from around the world still leave kings and pawns upon his grave.As I picture that small cemetery in Laugardælir Church near Selfoss, I cannot help thinking about the extraordinary distance, geographical and emotional, between Fischer’s birthplace and his final resting place. Here was a man who, at one of the tensest moments of the Cold War, gave pride and joy to millions of his countrymen, and who in his later years wrestled with demons perhaps not entirely of his choosing.Someone like that was owed more restraint, more understanding, from his own. He deserved a way back, and at last a place to lie among the people he had once made proud.Gens una sumus, chess says of itself: we are one family. Bobby Fischer lies far from home. But he does not lie among total strangers. He died as a citizen of a beautiful country that gave him refuge. The game he transformed, and the small island nation that loved him, made sure of that.
Article Summary: Aarav Dengla visits Bobby Fischer's grave in Iceland. Fischer was one of the greatest chess players ever. Dengla: Fischer's legacy extends far beyond his 1972 world championship win. He says Fischer withdrew into isolation and expressed paranoid, antisemitic views.

Article Title: Land mine blast survivor Soman Rana scripts golden CWG story with para shot put title
Article Text:
(From left) Soman Rana with coach Rakesh Singh Rawat and Shubham Juyal in Glasgow on Saturday

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Soman Rana had spent nearly a decade believing his sporting career was over.On Saturday, the Army para-athlete completed one of Indian sport’s most remarkable comebacks by winning India’s first-ever Commonwealth Games gold in the men’s F57 shot put in Glasgow.Rana, then serving with 2/8 Gorkha Rifles along the Line of Control in Jammu & Kashmir, suffered a mine blast injury on December 1, 2006. The explosion led to the below-knee amputation of his right leg, while his left leg was fractured badly enough to require a metal rod that remains in place even today.Now nearly two decades later since that day, nothing, it seems, can stop him. The 43-year-old from Bihar’s Gaya produced a best throw of 13.40m to win gold as training partner Shubham Juyal claimed silver with 13.28m, giving India its maiden gold and first-ever one-two finish in the men’s F57 shot put at CWG. Cameroon’s Cedric Azamdzi (12.57m) settled for bronze.The triumph was particularly significant for Rana, who was a national-level boxer before the accident abruptly ended his sporting career. He had trained alongside Vijender Singh and represented the Services Sports Control Board at 2005 Senior National Boxing Championships.“I had always been interested in sports. Before joining the Army, I used to play different games like volleyball and boxing.Even after joining the Army, I continued competing in boxing national championships. But after I was injured, I couldn’t play anymore,” Rana had said before the Games.According to his coach, Subedar Major Rakesh Singh Rawat, Rana’s achievement becomes even more remarkable considering the challenges he continues to overcome.“The biggest thing about Soman is that he is already 43. At this age, he is still producing personal best performances. He is also managing diabetes and high blood pressure while competing at the highest level,” Rawat told TOI.For Rawat, however, Rana’s determination defines him more than anything else.“For an Army man, his spirit is enough. He has already sacrificed his leg for the country, and that is what keeps him motivated,” said the coach, who has been coaching him for the last four years.The turnaround began in 2016 when Rana travelled to the Army’s Artificial Limb Centre in Pune to be fitted with a prosthetic leg. There he met fellow soldiers competing in para sports, who introduced him to Col Gaurav Dutta, then Officer-in-Charge of the Army Paralympic Node.Dutta immediately felt Rana had all the attributes to succeed in the throws. “Once I saw him and the kind of hulk he is, I told him that sitting shot put would suit him best,” Dutta recalled.Rana began training in 2017 but narrowly missed out on the 2018 Asian Para Games because of technical reasons. “He felt hard done by, but I told him to stay patient and that his chance would come,” Dutta said.His opportunity finally arrived three years later when he qualified for Tokyo Paralympics, where he finished fourth. He followed that up with a silver medal at 2023 Asian Para Games, narrowly missed another podium at Paris Paralympics, and then clinched bronze at 2025 World Para Athletics Championships. Yet, one major title remained missing.“Without hard work, there is no success. I’ll work as hard as I can and bring home the gold medal for the country,” Rana had said before leaving for Glasgow.On Saturday, he kept that promise. His 13.40m effort proved enough to hold off Juyal by just 12cm and write his name into the history books.Rana’s rise has also been backed by the Bihar govt’s sports scholarship policy and cash rewards under the state’s Khel Samman Samaroh, besides assistance through central government schemes.Currently ranked World No. 2, Rana, who has a PB of 15.17m, has already shifted his focus to Para Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, in October. Joining him there will be Nagaland’s Hokato Hotozhe Sema, the reigning World No. 1, giving India two genuine medal contenders in the event.
Article Summary: Soman Rana won India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold in the men's F57 shot put in Glasgow on Saturday. The 43-year-old suffered a mine blast injury on December 1, 2006, while serving with 2/8 Gorkha Rifles along the Line of Control in Jammu & Kashmir. The explosion led to the below-knee amputation of his right leg.

Former India wicketkeeper-batter Deep Dasgupta believes head coach Gautam Gambhir will be under pressure when India begin their two-match Test series against Sri Lanka in Galle on August 15. India have lost Test series against New Zealand, Australia and South Africa under Gambhir, and will now look to bounce back against Sri Lanka.Dasgupta said the pressure will not only be on Gambhir but also on captain Shubman Gill and the rest of the Indian team."As we are saying, two out of three series have been lost. So, there will be pressure. It is also important to say that all the names we are taking, everyone knows how to play under pressure, and they also know how to handle it. But there will be pressure on Shubman, the Indian players, and it is very, very important," Deep Dasgupta told IANS"Because they are talking about transition, it is very important to see a direction in the transition period. The transition started, let's say, after the New Zealand Test series; then came the England series and all of that. It started from there onwards. Somewhere, I feel that it is important to see a direction, and I am a little confused as to which direction we are going," he concluded.Dasgupta added that questions are bound to be asked if India's struggles continue."One thing is fair: questions will be asked of him (Gambhir).When the team does not play properly, questions will be asked individually. Obviously, the team's coach, captain, and everyone involved with the team will be asked questions because, if you look at it, we lost at home. After 2011-12, we lost the series in New Zealand, and we kept losing continuously," Deep Dasgupta said.Dasgupta also warned that India cannot afford to take any opposition lightly, especially with difficult away assignments coming up.The Sri Lanka series could play a key role in India's hopes of reaching the World Test Championship (WTC) final.India have nine Tests left in the current WTC cycle - away series in Sri Lanka - 2 Tests, away series against New Zealand - 2 Tests, home series against Australia - 5 Tests)."Well, firstly, there is no easy Test series, and especially right now, looking at the Indian Test side, which is going through a transition, there is not one easy Test match, no matter what happens.""Especially in Sri Lanka. Again, Sri Lanka has been a very difficult place to tour in the past, especially in these conditions right now. So, I think it's going to be interesting when looking at the WTC. I think there are nine Test matches left: five against Australia, two against Sri Lanka, and two against New Zealand. If I'm not wrong, roughly speaking, I think seven out of nine will have to be won to qualify for the WTC final.So, that in itself is a difficult task.""On top of that, you have Sri Lanka in Sri Lanka and New Zealand in New Zealand. These are difficult assignments. On top of that, if we look at it series by series, and if we don't count Afghanistan's one-off Test, then in the last three series, we have lost two, against New Zealand and South Africa. So, that is one thing. Obviously, that's why you can't take any series or opposition lightly at this time, in any condition," he said.
Article Summary: Former India wicketkeeper-batter Deep Dasgupta believes head coach Gautam Gambhir will be under pressure when India begin their two-match Test series against Sri Lanka in Galle on August 15. India have lost Test series. against New Zealand, Australia and South Africa under Gambhirs. India's chances of reaching the World Test Championship final are slim.

Article Title: Spiker-turned-goalkeeper Mohith eyes FIH World Cup splash
Article Text:
Goalkeeper HS Mohith (Image credit: Instagram)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: What began as an unwilling stint between the posts has turned into a calling. Young goalkeeper HS Mohith is now determined to impress at the upcoming FIH World Cup. If not under the bar, Mohith would have well been spiking or blocking the ball on a volleyball court.A shortage of goalkeepers at sports hostel in Hassan prompted the coach to ‘borrow’ Mohith from the volleyball team. Incidentally, the team did well in that tournament, and with his height being a disadvantage, Mohith was asked to continue with hockey.It took him barely two years to fall in love with the sport. Accepting his position, however, took longer. “I thought goalkeeping was a tough job. I went up to the coach and said I don’t want to be a goalkeeper, I want to be in forward line and score goals. It didn’t take him long to remind me that I was picked for the position and it would take them a while to train another goalkeeper,” Mohith told TOI during the World Cup preparatory camp at SAI Centre here.Disappointed but not defeated, the 24-yearold soon began looking at the role differently. “I realised how important a goalkeeper is. Unlike outfield players, who can sometimes get away with mistakes, a goalkeeper has nowhere to hide.I thrive under pressure and I started enjoying that responsibility,” he recalled.Mohith’s rise has been steady. A key member of India’s title-winning side at the 2023 Junior Asia Cup, he announced himself at last year’s Sultan Azlan Shah Cup before producing a composed display against Australia in the FIH Pro League, where he won the shootout for India.
Article Summary: Goalkeeper HS Mohith is now determined to impress at the upcoming FIH World Cup. A shortage of goalkeepers at sports hostel in Hassan prompted the coach to 'borrow' Mohith from the volleyball team. It took him barely two years to fall in love with the sport.

Article Title: Boxers pack a medal punch: Six Indians reach semifinals, assure record 10 medals
Article Text:
Sakshi Chaudhary

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s medal tally is set to swell. After the weightlifters did their bit, on Wednesday it was the boxers’ turn to take centre stage at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.So far, 10 Indian boxers have reached their respective semifinals, assuring themselves of at least a bronze medal each. Lovlina Borgohain had made the last four of the women’s 75kg category after receiving a bye in the draw, while Priya Ghanghas (60kg), Preeti Pawar (54kg) and Jadumani Singh (55kg) won their quarterfinal bouts on Tuesday.Boxing awards two bronze medals in each category, meaning every semifinalist is guaranteed a place on the podium.Wednesday, however, brought a six-medal windfall, beginning with Sakshi Chaudhary, who faced European Championships silver medallist Caitlin Fryers of Northern Ireland in the women’s 51kg quarterfinal. Fryers charged forward from the opening bell but Sakshi refused to be overpowered. She used her footwork well, landing clean punches before moving out of range to seal a 5-0 unanimous-decision victory.In the next bout, it was Arundhati Choudhary’s turn to shine in the women’s 70kg category. The first woman boxer from Rajasthan to compete at the CWG ensured she would not leave Glasgow empty-handed, although the contest was tougher than she may have anticipated.Her opponent, New Zealand’s Morgan Henderson, used to play rugby, and that aggression was evident in the ring. Henderson was docked a point but Arundhati matched her intensity and made the cleaner punches count to claim a 3-1 split-decision victory.In the men’s 60kg quarterfinal, world No. 5 and former World Youth champion Sachin Siwach registered a dominant 5-0 win over Botswana’s Treasure Moremi. In the men’s 80kg quarterfinal, Ankush Yadav advanced with a 5-0 unanimous-decision victory over Seychelles’ Jade Micock, while Narender Berwal completed the sweep by edging Samoa’s Michael Seko 3-2 in the men’s 90kg-plus quarterfinal.Later in the evening, Jaismine advanced to the women’s 57kg semifinals with 4-1 a win over Elise Glynn of England.India enjoyed a good day in the field too, with Tajinderpal Singh Toor and Samardeep Singh Gill progressing to the men’s shot put final. National record-holder Toor opened with 19.93m in Group A before improving to 20.14m to breach the automatic qualification mark of 20m. The twotime Asian Games champion then opted against taking his third throw.Gill qualified with his best throw of 19.95m in his first attempt in Group B. He followed it with 19.75m before fouling his third and final attempt.There was, however, disappointment in the women’s high jump final, where Asian U20 champion and national record-holder Pooja Singh finished eighth. She cleared 1.77m on her second attempt but failed to clear 1.82m. Weightlifter Sanjana Panchal was also eliminated early after failing all three snatch attempts at her opening weight of 94kg in the women’s 77kg event.
Article Summary: 10 Indian boxers have reached their respective semifinals, assuring themselves of at least a bronze medal each. It’s a lonely world out there for me. I can only see the face of my child during video calls. But to represent the nation is equally important,” Gulveer had said prior to his departure.The road to Glasgow wasn’t smooth. Ankle and knee sprains disrupted preparations while the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) asked him to return from his overseas base to compete at the InterState championships and prove his fitness. On his return, although he fell short of the upcoming Asian Games qualifying mark, Gulveer and coach Scott Simmons persisted with their programme at Colorado Springs, gradually rebuilding fitness and improving his timings. The dip in form in the lead up to the CWG caused concern, but Gulveer trained hard for the event.“I only focus on giving my best. I worked on improving my fitness and timing. Also, I don’t keep track of my national records and all,” he had said.Before joining the 23 Grenadiers in 2018, Gulveer had never dreamt of becoming an international athlete. “I started running seriously after joining the Army. Before that, I used to run only to get enrolled. I didn’t know anything about the CWG or Asian Games. I only came to know about them after joining the Army. ”His life changed almost accidentally in 2019. Stationed in Arunachal Pradesh, Gulveer prepared seriously for an inter-unit cross-country race, hoping a good performance would earn incentives and provide respite from demanding military duties. His 10km victory in 30:58 caught the eye of Army Sports Institute coach Younus Khan, who brought him to Pune and transformed a soldier into India’s premier distance runner.That mindset was evident in Glasgow. Amid rain, the reigning Asian 5,000m and 10,000m champion judged the pace superbly, adding another medal to a kitty that already boast of an Asian Games bronze and Asian Championship double gold.

NEW DELHI: Neeraj Chopra walks into the Commonwealth Games 2026 as India’s biggest athletics hope, but this may be far from a routine title defence.The Olympic champion and former world champion is returning to the Games after an eight-year gap, and the men’s javelin field in Glasgow is significantly stronger than the one he conquered in Gold Coast in 2018.Back then, Neeraj won gold with an 86.47m throw and looked a class apart. This time, he enters Scotstoun Stadium with questions around form, fitness and the depth of the competition. He missed Birmingham 2022 due to injury, and his 2026 season only began recently after recovering from a back problem.His first outing of the year at the Doha Diamond League showed both promise and rust. Neeraj produced a best throw of 85.69m, briefly moved into medal contention, but eventually finished fourth after two foul throws.For an athlete whose standards are now measured in 88m-plus and 90m territory, Doha suggested he is not yet at his absolute peak.The most obvious threat is Pakistan’s Arshad Nadeem. The rivalry between Neeraj and Arshad has become one of the defining stories in world athletics. Arshad owns a personal best of 92.97m, one of the greatest throws in history. His listed season best is only 78.47m, but that number is misleading because he has competed sparingly and has repeatedly shown he can produce huge throws in major championships.Grenada’s Anderson Peters is arguably the most dangerous athlete in the field on current form. The two-time world champion has a personal best of 93.07m and a season best of 86.38m, slightly better than Neeraj’s. Peters is known for his ability to throw consistently over 85m, which is often enough to stay in medal contention throughout a competition.Then there is Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage, the emerging force of the field. At just 23, he arrives with a personal and season best of 92.62m, making him statistically one of the biggest threats to gold. Unlike some rivals whose best marks came years ago, Rumesh has already crossed 92m this season.India also has Rohit Yadav, who has thrown 87.05m, while experienced names such as Keshorn Walcott (90.16m PB) and Julius Yego (92.72m PB) add further quality to the competition.The biggest challenge for Neeraj is not just one rival; it is the number of athletes capable of throwing beyond 85m. In 2018, he was clearly ahead of the field. In Glasgow, at least five athletes have personal bests above 90m, and several have season marks within touching distance of his own.Another factor is timing. Neeraj is still building rhythm after a back injury, and javelin is an event where technical sharpness matters as much as physical strength. A small loss of timing at release can cost two or three metres, which could be the difference between gold and bronze in a field this deep.The format also adds pressure. Qualification is on Thursday, with the final in the early hours of August 1 (IST). Athletes must manage recovery, rhythm and conditions across two rounds, and one poor series can end a medal challenge quickly.Neeraj remains the favourite because of his championship temperament. He has repeatedly delivered under pressure at the Olympics, World Championships and Asian Games. But unlike Gold Coast 2018, this will not be a competition he can win by reputation alone.If he throws 88m or more, a second Commonwealth gold is very likely. If he stays around the 85-86m range seen in Doha, Glasgow could turn into one of the most competitive and unpredictable javelin finals of his career.
Article Summary: Olympic champion and former world champion is returning to the Games after an eight-year gap. His first outing of the year at the Doha Diamond League showed both promise and rust. The most obvious threat is Pakistan’s Arshad Nadeem, who owns a personal best of 92.97m.

Article Title: CWG 2026: India’s jumpers overcome absence of regular trainers
Article Text:
Murali Sreeshankar (Image credit: PTI)

NEW DELHI: India’s jumpers have emerged among the standout performers in athletics at the Commonwealth Games, but their impressive results have come despite the absence of their coaches.High jumper Sarvesh Kushare clinched silver, while long jumpers Murali Sreeshankar and Lokesh Sathyanathan progressed to the final. High jumper Adarsh Ram finished fifth. Yet, throughout the competition, jumpers have largely been without their Indian coaches, who train them on a daily basis and guide them during competitions.Sarvesh’s coach Jithin Thomas is currently overseeing the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) training camp in Spala, Poland, which runs until Sept ahead of the Asian Games. Adarsh’s coach Sahana Kumari is with the Indian U-20 team for the World Athletics U-20 Championships in Eugene starting early next month. Sreeshankar’s father and coach, S Murali, a constant presence during his competitions, was not cleared to accompany him to Glasgow.The lack of dedicated coaching support became evident during the men’s high jump final. After withdrawing with a knee injury during the warm-up, Tejaswin Shankar stayed back to help Sarvesh from the sidelines.Noticing Sarvesh struggling with his approach, Tejaswin suggested a change in his run-up, advice that helped the eventual silver medallist regain rhythm. Tejaswin, himself, however, had no coach to support him through his own injury setback.According to the final athletics contingent cleared by the govt, chief coach Radhakrishnan Nair is the only Indian support staff personnel accredited with the contingent. The four foreign coaches accompanying the team are Scott Simmons (long distance), Jason Alexander Dawson (400m and relays), Ronald Gerd Weigel (race walking) and Yoandris Betanzos Francis (jumps).However, both Weigel and Betanzos have travelled as Extra Team Officials (ETOs), an accreditation that does not permit access to the competition venue and field of play. As a result, Betanzos can only watch the event from the stands and interact with athletes outside the venue, leaving India’s jumpers effectively without technical guidance during competition despite their strong performances.Raosaheb Jadhav, Sarvesh Kushare’s childhood coach, said, “Forget a coach, not a single support staff member was near the three Indian jumpers. All the other 15 jumpers had a coach or support staff member to correct their mistakes. During his two failed attempts, Sarvesh’s lower back touched the bar. Had there been a coach, he could have spotted the mistake on video and corrected it. Sarvesh could then have cleared 2.28m on his second attempt and won the gold. ”(inputs by Amit Sampat)
Article Summary: High jumper Sarvesh Kushare clinched silver, while long jumpers Murali Sreeshankar and Lokesh Sathyanathan progressed to the final. Yet, throughout the competition, jumpers have largely been without their Indian coaches, who train them on a daily basis and guide them during competitions.

Bangladesh squad for Australia Tests



Bangladesh have received a timely boost ahead of their two-Test series against Australia, with Litton Das returning to the squad after recovering from a left calf injury. The 31-year-old wicketkeeper-batter, who has been out of action since June, has completed his rehabilitation and has been declared fit to rejoin the national side. According to the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB), Litton will travel to Darwin on Sunday to link up with the squad ahead of the opening Test, which begins on August 13.Litton's return comes as welcome news for Bangladesh, who have already suffered setbacks in the lead-up to the series. The visitors will be without young fast bowler Nahid Rana, while Shoriful Islam is also unavailable for selection in the first Test because of injury. The experienced batter is now in contention for the series opener after making encouraging progress during his recovery programme.The upcoming series marks a significant moment for Bangladesh cricket as the team prepares to play a Test match in Australia for the first time in 23 years. Before the opening Test, Bangladesh will play a three-day warm-up match against a Cricket Australia XI in Darwin from August 6 to 8 to fine-tune their preparations.The first Test will be played at Marrara Cricket Ground in Darwin from August 13 to 17, while the second Test is scheduled for August 22 to 26 at Great Barrier Reef Arena in Mackay.Litton's return comes just days after he was named Bangladesh's ODI captain, adding another major responsibility to his international career. He replaces Mehidy Hasan Miraz, who led the side from June 2025 before stepping down following Bangladesh's 2-1 ODI series defeat to Zimbabwe.Miraz oversaw 20 ODIs during his tenure, winning 10 and losing nine, with Bangladesh securing home series victories over West Indies, Pakistan, Australia and New Zealand. Already serving as Bangladesh's T20I captain, Litton will now lead the team in the 50-over format as preparations gather pace for the 2027 ICC Men's Cricket World Cup. He has previously captained Bangladesh in seven ODIs, winning three of those matches.A veteran of 104 One-Day Internationals, Litton has scored 2,869 runs at an average of 30.84, including five centuries and 14 half-centuries.Najmul Hossain Shanto (captain), Soumya Sarkar, Shadman Islam, Tanzid Hasan, Mominul Haque, Mushfiqur Rahim, Amite Hasan, Jaker Ali Anik, Mehidy Hasan Miraz (vice-captain), Taijul Islam, Taskin Ahmed, Hasan Mahmud, Syed Khaled Ahmed, Ebadot Hossain, Musfik Hasan and Litton Das.

Following Ben Stokes' retirement from international cricket, England have turned to a familiar face to lead their Test side once again. While there had been widespread speculation that Harry Brook could take over the captaincy, the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has instead entrusted the role to Joe Root, who is set to begin his second stint as Test captain.Root, who stepped down from the role in 2022 after a five-year tenure, admitted he is relishing the opportunity to lead England again, believing his previous experience has better prepared him for the challenges ahead."Very much the same, to be honest. I don't think that will ever change. Whenever you get the opportunity to lead your country, it's all of those things. I guess, the unique and nice position that I find myself in this time is I've got a wealth of experience in terms of knowing what it takes, knowing what it looks like, having seen success with it and seeing some hard times as well,'' said Root in a video on the official ECB website."I've got a lot to fall back on and look at and help me and the team moving forward into this next little while. So, I don't think many captains get that opportunity and certainly not with the amount of games that I have behind me and the experiences that I've had in between now and that period there. So, I'm very much looking forward to it, very excited by the challenge that lies ahead and all the great cricket that we have coming up," Root added.Root captained England in 65 Test matches, registering 27 victories, the most by any England Test captain. Although he stepped down in 2022 after a difficult phase for the team, he has continued to be one of England's most dependable batters.The 35-year-old will officially begin his second stint as Test captain when England host Pakistan in the first Test of the series, starting August 19, as he looks to lead the side into a new chapter alongside new Test head coach Stephen Fleming.

West Indies will head into the decisive second Test against Pakistan full of confidence after a strong run of performances on home soil, with captain Roston Chase eager to turn the Caribbean into one of the toughest places for visiting teams to win.The series finale gets underway at Queen's Park Oval in Port of Spain on Sunday (August 2), with the hosts aiming to wrap up the contest after securing a commanding 90-run victory in the opening Test at Tarouba. Their recent home form has also included an emphatic innings-and-217-run win over Sri Lanka before the second Test of that series ended in a draw. Although a place in the World Test Championship final is no longer within reach, another victory would see the West Indies climb above England to seventh in the WTC standings.Chase believes the team's recent success is the result of a long-term plan that has started to pay off following a disappointing 2025 campaign, during which the Caribbean side managed only one win in nine Test matches."We had a clear plan after last year and identified where we wanted to be as a team," Chase said ahead of the match. "We're moving in the right direction, but we know there's another level to reach. Our focus is to stick to our processes, execute our plans, and give ourselves the best chance of winning this Test as well, " Chase said.The skipper also stressed the importance of making home conditions a major advantage."We've enjoyed some excellent results at home recently, and we want to keep building on that. Our goal is to make the Caribbean a very difficult place for visiting teams because we understand these conditions better than anyone else. Home advantage should count, and we want to continue using it to our benefit," he added.Pakistan arrive under pressure after suffering eight consecutive defeats in away Test matches, with losses coming on tours of Australia, South Africa, Bangladesh and now the West Indies. The pitch in Port of Spain is expected to provide more assistance to spin than the surface used for the first Test, which could influence team selections for both sides.West Indies are monitoring the fitness of Chase, whose off-spin adds balance to the bowling attack alongside lead spinner Jomel Warrican. The all-rounder was unable to bowl in the opening Test because of a finger injury but is optimistic about contributing with the ball in the series decider."The finger is improving," Chase said. "I managed to bowl a couple of overs in the nets today. There's still some discomfort, but I'm hopeful that by Sunday I'll be able to bowl a proper spell."Pakistan could respond to the spin-friendly conditions by bringing experienced off-spinner Sajid Khan into the playing XI after fielding Ali Usman as their only specialist spinner in the first Test. Salman Ali Agha also offers a useful spin option. West Indies, meanwhile, may consider handing a debut to left-arm spinner Joshua Bishop if they decide an extra frontline spinner is needed, setting the stage for an intriguing battle between the two spin attacks in the series decider.
Article Summary: West Indies take on Pakistan in second Test at Queen's Park Oval in Port of Spain. Hosts won the first Test by 90 runs at Tarouba. Captain Roston Chase wants to make the Caribbean a fortress for visiting teams. Pakistan have lost eight consecutive away Test matches.

Article Title: 'One day he could captain India': Selectors explain why 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi was named East Zone vice-captain
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The East Zone selectors have defended their decision to appoint 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi as vice-captain for the upcoming Duleep Trophy, describing the move as part of a long-term leadership plan rather than an indication of the team's pecking order.While Ishan Kishan 's appointment as captain was widely expected, the decision to hand the vice-captaincy to Sooryavanshi drew attention, especially with experienced campaigners such as Abhimanyu Easwaran Mohammed Shami and Mukesh Kumar also part of the squad.Sooryavanshi has featured in only eight first-class matches for Bihar, while Easwaran has played 113 first-class games and previously captained Bengal, India A and other representative sides.Explaining the reasoning behind the decision, Manish Vardhan, Jharkhand's representative on the East Zone selection committee, said the move was aimed at helping the youngster understand leadership from close quarters."We are not thinking about the present alone," Vardhan told Cricinfo. "A vice-captain gets to observe the captain closely and understand how a team is run. We wanted Vaibhav to be more involved with the group because we think it will help him as he develops."He's an extremely talented cricketer and is maturing steadily. Giving him this responsibility is another part of that process."Vardhan also clarified that Sooryavanshi's appointment does not automatically make him the stand-in captain if Kishan is unavailable.Although the selectors have not discussed that possibility, he suggested that an experienced player would likely take charge while Sooryavanshi continued as vice-captain.According to Vardhan, the committee's thinking behind appointing Kishan as captain was also based on long-term planning, with both Kishan and Sooryavanshi viewed as players capable of remaining in India's setup for many years."The vice-captain's role isn't about status," Vardhan said. "It's about what a young player can learn while working alongside the captain."Former Odisha cricketer and current selector-coach Pravanjan Mullick echoed those views, pointing out that Sooryavanshi has already served as Bihar's vice-captain in first-class cricket."Ishan is the captain and, as wicketkeeper, he is involved in every phase of the game," Mullick told Cricinfo. "This gives Vaibhav an opportunity to understand leadership without putting the responsibility of captaining the side on him. We want him to grow, maybe one day he could even captain India. That's the thought behind giving him the vice-captaincy."Cricinfo also reported that Easwaran was intentionally not considered for the vice-captain's role. The selection committee reportedly felt it would not be appropriate for the vastly experienced batter to serve as deputy to the comparatively inexperienced Kishan.
Article Summary: The East Zone selectors have defended their decision to appoint 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi as vice-captain for the upcoming Duleep Trophy. Manish Vardhan, Jharkhand's representative on the East Zone selection committee, said the move was aimed at helping the youngster understand leadership from close quarters. Ishan Kishan's appointment as captain was widely expected.

Article Title: Tamim Iqbal hopeful as BCB turns to government over India's Bangladesh tour
Article Text:
BCB president Tamim Iqbal (Image credit: BCB)

BCB seeks government's help

Geopolitical developments fuel fresh optimism

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) president Tamim Iqbal has stepped up efforts to ensure India's scheduled white-ball tour of Bangladesh goes ahead in September, with the board seeking government-level intervention to reassure New Delhi over the proposed series, according to a report by Cricbuzz.The development comes amid continued uncertainty over the six-match tour, which is expected to feature three ODIs and three T20Is, but has not yet received official confirmation.According to Cricbuzz, Tamim, accompanied by BCB Security Committee chairman Sayeed Ibrahim, met State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Thursday to request that the Bangladesh government initiate official communication with its Indian counterparts.The aim is to reassure India that Bangladesh is fully prepared to host the series in September.As per the report, Tamim acknowledged the meeting but declined to elaborate on the discussions.The report added that BCB officials have urged government representatives to engage directly with India, as the cricket board is still awaiting formal confirmation regarding the tour.Earlier this week, Tamim said the BCB remained hopeful that the series would take place, while acknowledging there were limits to what the board could do.He indicated that certain matters were beyond the BCB's control and would need to be addressed at the government level.The proposed Bangladesh-India series was originally scheduled for 2024 but was postponed following political unrest in Bangladesh. Although it was pushed to 2025, strained relations between the two cricket boards kept the tour in doubt.However, Cricbuzz reported there is renewed optimism that the series could finally take place, helped by recent diplomatic developments between the two countries.India has reportedly invited Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to attend the 18th BRICS Summit in September, while Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr. Khalilur Rahman recently said Dhaka and New Delhi had agreed to reset bilateral relations based on sovereign equality and mutual interests following a meeting with India's new High Commissioner.The report also noted that the BCB is yet to issue its Expression of Interest (EOI) despite completing the valuation process. Board officials are believed to be waiting for greater clarity on India's tour before proceeding with the next commercial steps.For now, Bangladesh cricket's top brass remains hopeful that diplomatic progress will translate into sporting action, with Tamim leading efforts to ensure one of the subcontinent's biggest bilateral series returns to the calendar.
Article Summary: BCB seeking government-level intervention to reassure New Delhi over proposed series. Tamim Iqbal met State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Thursday to request that the Bangladesh government initiate official communication with its Indian counterparts. The six-match tour is expected to feature three ODIs and three T20Is.

Article Title: India likely to play waiting game with Jasprit Bumrah for Sri Lanka Tests | Exclusive
Article Text:
Jasprit Bumrah

NEW DELHI: The Indian team management is likely to play the waiting game with seamer Jasprit Bumrah for the two-match Test series against Sri Lanka starting August 15 in Galle. TimesofIndia.com has learnt that while nothing serious is wrong with his left knee, the stakeholders are in no mood to rush the fast bowler for the crucial fixtures. He has already completed body conditioning sessions at the BCCI Centre of Excellence (CoE) since checking in on Thursday and will start bowling Saturday onwards. He is expected to increase the intensity of his training in the coming days.The 32-year-old was picked in the Shubman Gill-led squad for the series, but subject to fitness clearance. Bumrah missed the third ODI against England at Lord's due to an "impact injury" to his left knee but looked very sharp in the two fixtures he did play.It is reliably learnt that he was scheduled to receive an injection for a knee-related issue which had flared up during the business end of the T20 World Cup. Since then the knee was being handled with care during the IPL, and forced him to spend some time at the CoE before the T20 competition got underway. The BCCI medical team is understood to be aware of the sequence of events, the injection and the necessary recovery period."Selectors were thoroughly briefed. Bumrah was advised an injection by the BCCI medical team and had to rest for the following 8-10 days. The moment that period was over, he reached the CoE for assessment. He is yet to start bowling and the management will be given a better idea in the coming days," said a source tracking developments.As things stand, he is extremely unlikely to join the rest of the squad in Mumbai on August 3, for the scheduled August 4 departure, and a late call is expected regarding his travel to Sri Lanka. It wouldn't be a surprise if he directly links up with the squad in Galle ahead of the series opener. The management will make the final call depending on his progress in the next few days."It is too early to make that call. He will start bowling from Saturday, and the picture will become much clearer when he bowls full throttle. See it's not a batter we are dealing with. So, the assessment and other protocols are different.And with Bumrah, what's the need to take any chance? There are still 15 days for the Test. "So, fingers crossed," adds the source.India are scheduled to play a four-day practice match in Colombo from August 7 before assembling in Galle for the series opener from August 15. To keep their World Test Championship Final hopes alive, the Shubman Gill-led unit need to whitewash Sri Lanka 2-0.
Article Summary: Jasprit Bumrah has been ruled out of the two-match Test series against Sri Lanka. The fast bowler missed the third ODI against England at Lord's due to an "impact injury" to his left knee. India are scheduled to play a four-day practice match in Colombo from August 7 before assembling in Galle for the series opener from August 15.

Article Title: 'It’s just too soon': Rob Key reveals why England overlooked Harry Brook for Test captaincy
Article Text:
England's Joe Root runs between the wickets with teammate Harry Brook, left, during play on day one of the fifth and final Ashes cricket test between England and Australia in Sydney, Sunday, Jan. 4, 2026. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

England men's team managing director Rob Key has said it would have been "too soon" to make Harry Brook the new Test captain, explaining why the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) decided to bring back Joe Root instead.Root's return as full-time Test captain was confirmed on Thursday, along with the appointment of Stephen Fleming as England's new Test head coach after Ben Stokes retired from international cricket and Brendon McCullum stepped down from the role.Brook, who is England's white-ball captain, was made Test vice-captain before last year's Ashes and has been Stokes' deputy since then.However, he was not given the captaincy when Stokes missed the second Test against New Zealand earlier this summer, and has again missed out despite showing interest in the role.Key said he and Fleming had detailed discussions about the captaincy before the former New Zealand captain accepted the coaching job. Both felt Root was the right choice at this stage.“In an ideal world, what you want is the coach has a say in a captain,” Key explained. “Coach first, then you work out the captain – I explained that to anyone that had a chance of becoming England captain.“During the process, you are obviously speaking to different coaches and [the captaincy] is one of the questions you start asking, getting a feel for where they are at.Stephen and I spoke a lot about who we felt the best person was."Key said Brook still needs more time before taking charge of the Test side, while Root is ready to lead again.“It’s just too soon for Harry Brook. This feels the right time for Joe Root. He has the chance to work with what I believe is the best coach that will complement him as well. Those two will be a great complementary pairing to take England forward. He is our best ever batter, and now has the chance to captain the side without any of the stuff he had to deal with last time. I’m just so glad he gets that chance," Key said as quoted by The Independent.Root had earlier admitted that he developed an "unhealthy relationship" with the captaincy during his previous spell, which ended after England managed only one win in 17 Tests during a period affected by the Covid pandemic.The 35-year-old enjoyed working with McCullum during England's recent Test series against New Zealand and will now begin a new partnership with Fleming, who is widely respected for his leadership during his playing career.Even though Brook missed out this time, Key said the Yorkshire batter remains England's long-term captaincy option.“I think he is still developing as a player and a person, really,” the former Kent and England batter said of Brook. “The Test match job is the biggest job in cricket in England. I think that it is perfect now with Joe where he can take this ship forward as the most senior player by a long way, and Harry can continue on the project he has done in the white-ball job, and continue learning to become an outstanding leader of a cricket team. "“You’ve got the 2027 World Cup, all of those things. At some stage, Harry Brook will be an outstanding Test captain of England cricket. It just doesn’t feel the time was right now.”
Article Summary: Rob Key says it would have been 'too soon' for Harry Brook to become England Test captain. England and Wales Cricket Board decided to bring back Joe Root instead. Brook was made Test vice-captain before last year's Ashes and has been Ben Stokes' deputy since then.

Article Title: 'Brilliant story if he does': England leave door open for Ben Stokes' Ashes return
Article Text:
Ben Stokes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

England men's team managing director Rob Key has not ruled out the possibility of Ben Stokes returning to international cricket before next year's Ashes, saying "anything is possible with Ben."Stokes stepped down as England's Test captain and retired from international cricket after England lost the Test series to New Zealand 2-1 in June. That defeat came after a 4-1 Ashes series loss to Australia during the previous winter.The 35-year-old had also been ruled out of the second Test against New Zealand after breaching a midnight curfew while celebrating England's victory in the opening Test.There was speculation after the incident that Stokes was unhappy with the way he had been treated by England's management. On Thursday, England brought back Joe Root as Test captain and appointed Stephen Fleming as Brendon McCullum 's replacement as Test head coach.Asked if Stokes could return in time for next year's Ashes, Key told Sky Sports News: "It would be a brilliant story if he does."Speaking after Fleming's appointment, Key said Stokes had given no indication that he wanted to return but admitted he would not be surprised if that changed."It would be a brilliant story if he does," Key told Sky Sports News. "He hasn't [indicated a change of heart], but I wouldn't be surprised.Anything is possible with Ben."When asked if Stokes had damaged his relationship with England by announcing his retirement during the fourth day of the Trent Bridge Test, Key said: "No, not at all. Not as far as I'm concerned."Since retiring, Stokes has focused on playing for Durham. He scored a century on his return last week in a One-Day Cup match, which was played on the opening day of The Hundred.As long as Stokes continues playing domestic cricket, discussions about a possible England comeback before the 2027 Ashes are expected to continue.
Article Summary: England men's team managing director Rob Key has not ruled out the possibility of Ben Stokes returning to international cricket. Stokes stepped down as England's Test captain and retired from international cricket after England lost the Test series to New Zealand 2-1 in June. The 35-year-old had also been ruled out of the second Test against New Zealand after breaching a midnight curfew.

Article Title: CWG 2026: From selection uncertainty to silver, Jadumani Singh's remarkable rise
Article Text:
Jadumani Singh (left) with Rishikanta Singh in Glasgow

TOI

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Until a few days before Commonwealth Games, Jadumani Singh wasn’t even sure he would board the flight to Glasgow.The uncertainty over his inclusion in India’s squad had left the Manipuri boxer under immense pressure. On Saturday, he answered those doubts by winning silver in the men’s 55kg category, becoming the first male boxer from Manipur to win a Commonwealth Games medal after 12 years.“For an athlete, nothing is more painful than training with complete dedication and then not knowing if you’ll even get the chance to compete. That creates tremendous mental pressure,” his coach Sarita Devi toldon Saturday.“He had gone through a similar situation earlier when he moved to the 55kg category from 50kg. There was uncertainty over whether he would be allowed to compete. This time, too, before Glasgow, he was under pressure because he didn’t know if he would get to compete.”While the medal was won inside the ring, the week in Glasgow was made easier by one familiar face outside the ropes. Weightlifter Rishikanta Singh, who won silver in the men’s 60kg event, spent much of his free time with Jadumani, keeping his fellow Manipuri’s spirits high amid the pressures of competition.Rishikanta had to leave Glasgow before Saturday’s boxing final but was overjoyed by his friend’s achievement. “I don’t see us as individual athletes, I see us as a team,” Rishikanta said before boarding his flight back home.Sarita said Jadumani’s run to the final was built as much on preparation as execution and she also helped out as much as possible despite being far away. That planning, however, was in stark contrast to the carefree persona Jadumani displayed inside the ring. His celebrations and playful gestures quickly became a talking point, but Sarita insists they were simply an extension of his personality.“That’s just his personality. Since childhood, he has been a very cheerful and playful person. He is always joking with people, and that naturally comes out in the ring as well. Sometimes it may look like he’s showing off, but that’s simply how he is,” she said.Long before Sarita was helping him decode opponents in Glasgow, Jadumani was just another energetic youngster training in the house of Chinglen Meitei in Imphal.Chinglen, who coached him for nearly two years, still remembers the first day the youngster walked in with his uncle. “The first thing I noticed was his courage. He wasn’t afraid of anyone,” Meitei said. “He was a mischievous boy and always ready for a fight. I felt if that energy was channelled in the right direction, he could become a very good boxer.”The former national-level boxer believes discipline, more than talent, has taken Jadumani this far.“Even today, before important bouts, he video calls me for advice. Before one of his fights in Glasgow, I suggested a few tactical changes and he followed them. That’s his biggest quality. Whenever a coach tells him something, he listens,” Chinglen added.Having watched the youngster rise from training in a modest neighbourhood setup to a Commonwealth Games podium, Chinglen said the achievement was deeply personal.Sarita, meanwhile, believes Glasgow is only the beginning. “He has improved tremendously and shown his commitment. But now he has to remain consistent. Many athletes do well initially but struggle to reach the Olympic level. I don’t want that to happen with him,” Sarita said.“Our target is the Asian Games and, ultimately, the Los Angeles Olympics. He is still young, he listens, works hard and has the courage to compete against anyone. I’ll continue to support him because our dream is to win an Olympic gold medal for India.”
Article Summary: Jadumani Singh is the first male boxer from Manipur to win a Commonwealth Games medal after 12 years. The Manipuri boxer won silver in the men’s 55kg category. His coach Sarita Devi says Glasgow is only the beginning.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Tejaswin Shankar battles injury to win historic decathlon bronze
Article Text:
India's Tejaswin Shankar (AP/PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Five days ago, after painfully pulling out of the high jump because of knee trouble, Tejaswin Shankar’s voice cracked and his eyes welled up.“I’ll try to give my best in the next two days,” he said then. The decathlon loomed ahead. At that point, he feared his Commonwealth Games campaign was over. His heart, though, kept a sliver of hope alive.The next four days were anything but easy. Once the decathlon started, Shankar knew there would be only two possible outcomes: agony or glory.On Friday night, the first Indian to win a high jump medal at the Commonwealth Games four years ago became the first Indian athlete to win a decathlon medal at the event. It was a bronze, but one that carried the weight of gold.Before the decathlon began, Shankar had two difficult decisions to make.“The first choice was made by withdrawing from the high jump event. He felt a little twinge in his knee during the practice jumps. When he took his first jump, he realised he had to withdraw,” said sports surgeon Dr Dinshaw Pardiwala, chief medical officer of Team India in Glasgow.“The second choice was to participate in the decathlon event. He considered the possibility of it affecting his chances of competing in the Asian Games . Once he decided to go ahead, we had 48 hours to prepare him for the gruelling event.We gave him medicines, did physiotherapy and also got a hyperbaric oxygen therapy chamber, which may not have any evidence of healing such injuries, but it did give him some confidence,” Dr Pardiwala told TOI.Shankar finished with 7,976 points across the 10 events over two days, despite carrying a chronic patellar tendon issue. The medal was not just a tribute to willpower; it was the product of a carefully managed plan.The Asian Games silver medallist knew the track events would be the toughest part of the programme. He did the bare minimum there to stay in contention, starting with a fifth-place finish in his 100m heat in 10.96s. Then came the long jump, where he produced 7.82m for 1,015 points.In a beautiful twist of fate, the event that had ended in tears a few days earlier, the high jump, yielded his biggest haul, as he cleared 2.15m for 944 points.A solid run in the 110m hurdles, where he clocked 14.41 seconds, kept him in the top four. The Kansas State University graduate then produced another personal best in the discus throw with 40.44m, before delivering a season’s best 53.12m in the javelin.
Article Summary: Shankar finished with 7,976 points across the 10 events over two days, despite carrying a chronic patellar tendon issue. The Asian Games silver medallist knew the track events would be the toughest part of the programme. The Kansas State University graduate produced another personal best in the discus throw with 40.44m.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu secure triple jump silver and bronze
Article Text:
CWG 2026: Praveen Chithravel wins silver, Selva Prabhu takes bronze in men's triple jump

Four years ago, triple jumper Praveen Chithravel had to return heartbroken from the Birmingham Commonwealth Games after missing bronze by 0.03m. In Glasgow, he’s ensured that the excess baggage on his return flight home would contain only joy.On Saturday, the Tamil Nadu athlete leaped to 16.58m to claim the silver medal in the men’s event.Selva Prabhu Thirumaran, also from Tamil Nadu, jumped to his season’s best effort of 16.52m to take a bronze for himself. The gold was won by Jamaica’s Jordan Scott, who leaped to 16.72m in his fourth attempt.Praveen had crossed 16.89m in Birmingham, but still finished fourth. On Saturday, he started with a jump of 16.05m but dropped to 15.64m in his second attempt.He forced a recalibration in the third attempt with a 16.31m jump. But his best effort, and the medal-winning one, came in his fourth jump as he touched 16.58m. His fifth jump saw him at 16.40m, while his last jump was a foul. Selva’s medal-winning effort came in his fifth jump.In the women’s 10,000m race walk, Priyanka Goswami finished fourth with a season’s best timing of 45:53.93. The other Indian in the walk, Ravina, was disqualified after completing 4000m.Judoka Unnati Sharma clinched the bronze medal in the women’s 63kg event after defeating South Africa’s Skye Knoester by ippon, wrapping up the contest in just 1 minute and 7 seconds.
Article Summary: Four years ago, triple jumper Praveen Chithravel had to return heartbroken from the Birmingham Commonwealth Games after missing bronze by 0.03m. On Saturday, the Tamil Nadu athlete leaped to 16.58m to claim the silver medal in the men’s event. Selva Prabhu Thirumaran, also from Tamil Nadu, jumped to his season's best effort of 16.52m to take a bronze for himself.

Article Title: CWG 2026: India win seven boxing golds as Preeti Pawar sets the tone
Article Text:
Glasgow: India's Preeti Pawar, in blue, reacts after winning a gold medal (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Being the first off the blocks has its advantages. It can cause the jitters too.On Saturday, Preeti Pawar was the first to start the gold medal bout of the 10 Indians who had made the boxing finals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Friday. The Haryana boxer would have felt those butterflies in the stomach, but more than that, Preeti knew she had that sting in her punches, a familiar, happy place, that would open the door for the gold rush that followed for India after her 5-0 win in the women’s 54kg final.And that’s what happened.The thoughtful Preeti, who loves to sketch in her me-time, defeated Canada’s Scarlett Delgado 5-0 to open India’s gold account in boxing.“I was not nervous, but conscious of the fact that my bout was first and the result would have an impact on my teammates. But I was also sure of winning it and giving the start that India needed,” Preeti told TOI.Taking a leaf from Preeti’s emphatic opener, four more Indians, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas and Arundhati Choudhary, won gold by clinching their respective finals.It could have been an India Perfect 10, but the promising Jadumani Singh of Manipur had to settle for silver in the men’s 55kg final.There was further disappointment for Tokyo Games bronze medallist Lovlina Borgohain, who had got a bye and a direct entry in the semifinals, as she lost her final 1-4 in split decision against Australia’s Emma-Sue Greentree in the women’s 75kg final.Preeti, who had participated at the 2024 Paris Olympics and won gold at last year’s World Cup Finals, along with taking the Asian Championships top medal this year, didn’t have any trouble in beating the Canadian in a unanimous decision.In the second bout, current World No. 1 and World Champion Jaismine found a tough challenger in last edition’s champion Michaela Walsh of Northern Ireland. After taking the first round on a split decision, Jaismine focused on her defence and landed some clean punches to take the next two rounds unanimously and win with a 5-0 scoreline.In the men’s event, Jadumani, who met a taller opponent again in Jye Dixon of Australia, struggled in making his punches land. Jadumani lost 0-5.Later, Sakshi brought the gold campaign back on track by registering a 5-0 win against England’s Ruby White in the women’s 51kg medal round.Priya won a tough fight with a 4-1 split decision against Canada’s Marie-Bathoul Al-Ahmadieh in the women’s 60kg final.The ever-smiling Arundhati didn’t allow herself to get dominated by England’s Chantelle Reid. The Kota boxer won gold after a 5-0 victory.In the men’s 60kg bout, Namibia’s Tryagain Morning Ndevelo troubled Sachin Siwach with his reflexes and attempts to take the bout after getting the judges’ nod in the first round.However, the Indian fought back to claim the second round with a split decision, and the bout too with a 3-2 split verdict.In the men’s 80kg final, Ankush Panghal defeated England’s Dimeji Shittu 4-1 to win India’s seventh gold in boxing.In the last bout, Narender Berwal lost 0-5 to England’s Damar Thomas.
Article Summary: Preeti Pawar was the first to start the gold medal bout of the 10 Indians. The Haryana boxer defeated Canada’s Scarlett Delgado 5-0. Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas and Arundhati Choudhary also won gold.

Article Title: Misses CWG gold, makes big Asian Games promise: India boxer Narender Berwal vows strong comeback
Article Text:
Narender Berwal (Image credit: X)
